title: Sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock, urosepsis and bacteremia
question: From this hospital discharge summary, assign the ICD-10-CM codes for the sepsis, severe sepsis or septic shock only (not the local infection or the organ dysfunction). If none applies, choose 'no code'.
note:
Admission Date: 05/10/2026
Discharge Date: 05/20/2026

Reason for Admission: Sepsis secondary to pneumonia.

Vitals:
Temperature: 101.4 F (on admission)
Blood Pressure: 82/50 mmHg (on admission)
Heart Rate: 115 bpm
Respiratory Rate: 26 breaths/min
SpO2: 91% on room air

Recent Labs:
WBC: 16.5 x 10^9/L
Lactic Acid: 4.2 mmol/L
Creatinine: 1.3 mg/dL
Hemoglobin: 11.8 g/dL
Platelets: 145,000/mm3

Review of Systems:
The patient reports productive cough, shortness of breath, and generalized fatigue. She denies chest pain, abdominal pain, or neurological deficits.

Social History:
The patient lives at home with her spouse. She is a retired teacher and is a former social smoker (quit 20 years ago).

Family History:
Mother had hypertension and stroke. Father had type 2 diabetes.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 79-year-old woman who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory distress and fever. She was admitted with sepsis due to pneumonia. During the initial hours of admission, her blood pressure declined significantly, and she was diagnosed with septic shock. She required the initiation of vasopressors to maintain adequate perfusion. Cultures were obtained, but no organism grew from the samples. She was managed with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Over several days, her hemodynamic status stabilized, and she was successfully weaned off the vasopressors. Her oxygen requirements decreased, and her symptoms improved significantly. She remained stable and was deemed ready for discharge.

Discharge Diagnoses:
1. Sepsis
2. Pneumonia
3. Septic shock

Discharge Medications:
1. Amoxicillin 500mg every 8 hours (oral)
2. Lisinopril 10mg daily
3. Atorvastatin 20mg daily

Follow-up:
The patient will follow up with her primary care physician in 7 days for a wound check and a repeat chest X-ray. She was instructed to return to the emergency department immediately if she experiences worsening shortness of breath or high fever.

Electronically signed,
D. Kowalski, MD
05/20/2026
explanations: Septic shock is severe sepsis with circulatory failure: A41.9 plus R65.21.

distractors.why: Septic shock is documented: R65.21, not R65.20.

style.document: Write a hospital discharge summary with sections: Admission Date, Discharge Date, Reason for Admission, Hospital Course, Discharge Diagnoses, Discharge Medications, Follow-up. It is the inpatient record of this hospital stay, not an office note.
